description: Hello I am a student at UPenn in scientific computing. I'm looking for teammates to work on the farming challenge with me. I'm happy to meet in person as well!
summary:
We developed a tool evaluating 2020 - 2024 crop rotations across the United States focusing on soybeans and corn. We evaluate the overall margins a farmer could expect with several rotation strategies based on historical crop yields, costs and sales figures. As a fun addition to this project, we trained several machine learning models to predict crop yields based on NASA POWER data and crop rotations and incorporated this into the analysis. 

Github Link to the Project Code is Here: 
https://github.com/Simon-Higgins/Nasa-Farms-Philadelphia
details:
This dashboard allows a user to focus on a particular county and see how different crop rotation strategies performed from 2020-2024 for corn and soybeans. The user can filter for the strategy they are interested in and see how it compares to other rotation strategies by overall margin/acre.

There is also a score element that scores a strategy’s overall profitability and water usage.

The benefit of the tool is that it uses a predictive yield in its margin calculation that could be applied to predicting crop yields in any county in the united states given NASA POWER data. (Currently the project runs that yield estimator on historical data but it is extensible with the algorithm we use to predicting future yields and thus future margins)

As it stands, the project is not a useful predictive tool for future years and more an interesting look at historical rotation strategies but given some more time it could easily be adapted into a very effective crop rotation predictor tool. We used python to develop the project, streamlit as the simple frontend visualization tool and sklearn for the machine learning elements.

The project is creative in the sense that we had to figure out how we wanted to actually look at crop margins and predict them. This involved a lot of thought around how to predict crop yields, crop costs broken down by county/year and crop inputs.

We considered crop rotations and various temperature, soil wetness, humidity and wind speed datapoints to predict crop yields across several years and then combined this with cost and sales data to come up with predicted margins.
